The sense "rapacious, extortionate person" arose by association with obsolete piller (“plunderer”). See Modern Norman cattepeleuse.

parole.significato: A drink given to the sick, consisting of ale or wine, bread, and eggs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English caudel, from Old Northern French caudel, from Medieval Latin caldellum, diminutive of Latin caldus, calidus (“warm”).

parole.significato: A large bowl-shaped pot used for boiling over an open flame.
parole.testo: From Middle English caudroun, borrowed from Old Northern French caudron, ultimately from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), from Latin caldus (“hot”). parole.significato: To drive oakum into the seams of a ship's wooden deck or hull to make it watertight.
parole.testo: From Old Northern French cauquer, from Late Latin calicāre (“to fill in with limestone, caulk”), derived from calx (“limestone, chalk”). Related to calx, cauk, chalk, and calculus.

parole.significato: Capable of being changed.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaungeable, from Old Northern French chaungeable, from Late Latin cambiāre (“to change”), equivalent to change + -able.

parole.significato: A long outer garment worn over the shoulders covering the back; a cape, often with a hood.
parole.testo: From Middle English cloke, from Old Northern French cloque (“travelling cloak”), from Medieval Latin clocca (“travelers' cape, literally “a bell”, so called from the garment’s bell-like shape”), of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos, ultimately imitative. Doublet of cloche and clock.

parole.significato: A closed box in which the body of a dead person is placed for burial.
parole.testo: From Middle English coffyn, from Old Northern French cofin (“sarcophagus", earlier "basket, coffer”), from Latin cophinus (“basket”), a loanword from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “a basket”). Doublet of coffer. Displaced native Old English þrūh.

parole.significato: The decayed remains of organic matter that has rotted into a natural fertilizer.
parole.testo: From Middle English compost, from Old Northern French compost (“a mixture of leaves, manure, etc., for fertilizing land, also a condiment”), from Latin compositus (“composed”), from componere. Doublet of compote, which was taken from modern French, composite, and kompot.

parole.significato: A solemn assembly or council.
